Where the data came from. The search index holds {0} entries built from the codebook. An entry is a single question, a question paired with one of its response options, or a family of sibling questions that share a stem. The retriever renders each request as one line of text, scores it against every entry, and returns the closest. No language model takes part in that step. The test set holds {1} requests with a known reference entry and {2} requests written about constructs the codebook does not measure. The {3} cover {4} codebook entries, each phrased {5} ways, so every count out of {6} below counts requests, not distinct entries: each block of {7} requests is {8} phrasings of one entry, and {9} entries were tested in all. A language model wrote the {10} after seeing the reference wording, so every hit rate below is optimistically biased: an upper bound, not an estimate of field performance. The {11} absent requests are the only part of this evaluation held out from every development decision, and a language model wrote those too. For {12} of the {13} entries the reference is a family of sibling questions, and a hit anywhere in the family counts as correct. What each number counts. Top-1 accuracy is how often the reference entry ranked first: {14} of {15}. Another {16} reached the right construct but the wrong question, and those count as misses, not partial credit. AUROC, answerable vs absent is discrimination between answerable and absent requests: how well the similarity score separates the two groups. AUROC, correct vs wrong is discrimination between correct and incorrect top matches, using the same score, and it is a much harder task. Threshold is the score below which the system abstains instead of guessing.

A short description of something a researcher wants to measure, like what you would type into the box at the top of this page. A language model wrote every request here from a single codebook entry, and that entry is its reference standard, so "first" means the source entry ranked at the top of the list.{0} {1} n counts requests, not entries, so a bar at n={2} rests on a single entry: the smallest samples carry the least evidence, however long their bars look. No requests fall on {3}, so those topics have no bar. Search performance there is unmeasured, which is not the same as good.

Why one score discriminates so differently on the two tasks. Each figure here is an upper median: at least half the requests in its group scored at or below it, and the figure is one of the observed scores. On an even-sized group it is the upper of the two middle values, not their mean, which is why it is not called the median. An absent request: nothing in the codebook is close, so the best match is weak — typically {0}, against {1} for a request the codebook can answer. The two distributions barely overlap, which is why that area is high. Answerable but wrong: a close entry exists, but it is not the reference entry. A correct top match scores {2} and an incorrect one {3}, so the two distributions lie on top of each other. The highest-scoring incorrect match reaches {4}, above the typical correct one. The score measures how similar the best entry is to the request, not whether it is the entry you meant, so it cannot separate a confident wrong answer from a confident right one.
